The normal distribution

The normal distribution is the familiar bell-shaped curve that describes many measurements — heights, test scores, manufacturing errors. It is fixed by two numbers: the mean μ (the centre) and the standard deviation σ (the width). This calculator finds the probability that a normal variable falls below, above or between values, and works backwards to find the value at a given percentile.

Try changing the input

Compute P(μ−σ<X<μ+σ) for any μ and σ: it is always about 0.6827. Normal probabilities depend only on how many standard deviations you are from the mean.

Formulas

f(x)=1σ2π e−(x−μ)22σ2P(X<a)=Φ(a−μσ)
P(X>a)=1−Φ(za)P(a<X<b)=Φ(zb)−Φ(za)xp=μ+Φ−1(p) σ

Φ is the cumulative distribution function of the standard normal distribution — the values printed in a z-table. Here it is computed directly to about 15 significant digits.

Worked example

IQ scores: μ=100, σ=15. Find P(X<120).

Step 1 — Standardise

z=120−10015≈1.3333

Step 2 — Look up Φ(z)

P(X<120)=Φ(1.3333)≈0.9088

About 90.9% of people score below 120.

Assumptions, domain and rounding

  • The variable is assumed to follow a normal distribution with the given μ and σ>0.
  • For percentiles, p must be strictly between 0 and 1 (enter 0.95 for the 95th percentile).
  • Because the distribution is continuous, "<" and "≤" give the same probability.
  • Probabilities are rounded to 6 decimal places; very small tail probabilities are shown in scientific notation.
